Lessons.Title: Systems of Linear Equations and Their Solutions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: distinguish linear systems with no solution, exactly one solution or infinitely many solutions using their equation structure and graphs. Original Edulytiks material aligned with Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L17, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/17/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Building On 8.EE.C.8 and HSA-CED.A.4; Addressing HSA-CED.A.3, HSA-REI.C.6.

Original three-system comparison: A has y=2x+1 and y=2x+5; same slope but different intercepts => parallel lines, no pair satisfies both. B has y=3x−2 and 2y=6x−4; identical lines => all pairs (x,3x−2) are solutions. C has y=x+1 and y=−x+5; equalizing gives x+1=−x+5 ->2x=4,x=2,y=3, one intersection.

Emphasize that infinitely many solutions means infinitely many ordered pairs, not infinitely many arbitrary x/y choices. If two standard-form equations are multiples of one another, they represent the same line; if their slopes agree and distinct intercepts remain, they never meet.

Student task: graph the three systems, classify and justify each solution cardinality by both algebra and visual features, provide one valid pair for the infinite system, and critique any wrong classification. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, max 8): correct classifications, tested solution pairs, correct slope/intercept reasoning and coherent graphical explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel lines
KeyConcepts.Definition: Distinct nonvertical lines with equal slopes and different intercepts do not intersect.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare the fully simplified slope-intercept forms.
KeyConcepts.Example: y=2x+1 and y=2x+5 have no common pair.

KeyConcepts.Title: Coincident lines
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equivalent equations graph the same line and share infinitely many ordered pairs.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check that multiplying/rearranging produces the other equation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Single crossing
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different slopes produce exactly one intersection for two nonvertical lines.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Set y expressions equal to solve.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify parallel system
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve y=2x+1, y=2x+5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
Steps: Distinct intercepts 1 and 5 with equal slope 2 imply parallel lines.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recognize infinitely many solutions
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve y=3x−2, 2y=6x−4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
Steps: Divide the second equation by nonzero 2.
Every point on that line satisfies both.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Infinitely many ordered-pair solutions on y=3x−2.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both equations yield the same set.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find unique intersection
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve y=x+1, y=−x+5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the full system and verify the resulting pair in both original equations.
Steps: Add x and subtract 1 to get 2x=4.
WorkedExamples.Check: Slopes +1 and −1 differ, so one intersection.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling equivalent equations two separate intersection lines
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare all coefficients or simplify forms.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling a parallel-line pair one solution because lines look close
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: They never meet when slopes match and intercepts differ.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the exact equations, not a pixel sketch.

SummaryPoints: Linear systems may have 0, 1 or infinitely many solutions.
Parallel distinct lines yield none; identical lines yield infinitely many.
Differently sloped lines have one intersection.
Graph interpretation and number of solutions require justification.
